docs: Add Javadocs and align Java style
commitResults.messageBody:
Bobby's core classes expose public methods and parsing helpers that benefit from concise API documentation.

Add missing Javadocs for the app entry point and non-trivial private helpers. Standardize import grouping and Javadoc tag punctuation so future code follows the SE-EDU Java coding standard without changing behavior.

commitResults.messageBody:
Future Java changes need a reusable project-local reference for the SE-EDU coding standard.

Add a seedu-java-coding-standard skill and update AGENTS.md so agents use it for Java edits in this repository.

Future commits need a reusable project-local reference for the SE-EDU Git conventions.

Add a seedu-git-standard skill and update AGENTS.md so agents use it when proposing commit messages or changing Git history.

Users need a way to locate tasks without scanning the full list.

Add a find command that searches task descriptions case-insensitively and displays matching tasks in list order.

commitResults.messageTitle: Package JavaFX libraries in the JAR
commitResults.messageBody:
The generated JAR depends on JavaFX classes used by the GUI.

A normal JAR can fail on computers that do not have JavaFX installed,
because those third-party classes are not available at runtime.

Let's add the OpenJFX runtime dependencies for Windows, macOS, and Linux
so Shadow packages the GUI libraries into the executable JAR.

Including all three platform classifiers keeps the JAR usable across the
operating systems expected by the course, at the cost of a larger
artifact.

Core command handling, storage parsing, task operations, and FXML loading
rely on several internal assumptions being true.

When those assumptions are violated, the failure should point to the
broken contract near the code that depends on it instead of surfacing
later as a less helpful exception.

Let's add Java assert statements for assumptions such as:

* commands and task lists are non-null before handling
* task indexes are valid before mutation
* FXML controls are injected before GUI handlers use them
* task descriptions, task types, and dates are non-null

Enable assertions for the Gradle run task so these checks are active when
the application is launched during development.

Bobby has separate command-handling paths for the console UI and the
JavaFX GUI. Both paths decide which command was entered, update the task
list, save changes, and produce almost identical response text.

Duplicated command flow makes the code harder to read and maintain. A
future command update can easily change one interface while leaving the
other with outdated behavior.

Let's route the console UI through the same response-generation method
used by the GUI and let Ui print multi-line responses generically.

This keeps command parsing and task side effects in one place while
leaving Ui responsible only for console input and output.

Bobby.handleCommand handles every user command in one branching method. It recognizes commands, parses arguments, mutates the task list, saves data, and formats responses in the same block.

That concentration of responsibilities makes the method harder to scan as more commands are added. The code quality guide recommends keeping methods short and structuring code so related steps read logically.

Let's extract focused helpers for list, find, mark, unmark, delete, and add command handling. Keep the dispatcher responsible for routing only, while each helper owns the workflow for one command.

This keeps the refactoring behavior-preserving and avoids introducing a larger command abstraction before the application needs it.

Storage.parseTask and its helpers read the save-file fields using
literal indexes, field counts, task type codes, and status codes.

Those values are part of Bobby's storage format. Raw literals make the
parser harder to read and easy to change inconsistently.

Let's name the storage field positions, allowed field counts, type codes,
and status codes before using them in the parser.

Keeping the constants local to Storage makes the format clearer without
changing the public task model or adding a broader abstraction.

TaskList stores tasks in a mutable list and exposes that list through
its public API. Callers can depend on ArrayList and can mutate the task
collection without using TaskList operations.

That weakens encapsulation and makes the class harder to reason about.
The code quality guide recommends keeping code easy to understand, and a
clear class boundary helps readers see where task mutations are meant to
happen.

Let's accept and return List at TaskList boundaries, copy constructor
input, and return a copy from asList. Update the affected callers and
tests to use the interface type.

This keeps TaskList simple while making accidental external mutation less
likely.

Parser repeats the same validation pattern when it reads required command segments. Several methods substring, trim, check for an empty value, and throw a command-specific BobbyException.

That repetition makes the parser longer and scatters one parsing rule across multiple methods. The code quality guide recommends keeping code readable and avoiding duplicated logic when a small extraction makes the intent clearer.

Let's extract the required-segment validation into one helper and keep each command parser focused on the structure of the command it handles.

This is a local helper instead of a broader parsing abstraction because the parser only needs one shared rule here: required text between known command separators must not be empty.

Bobby owns both chatbot response generation and the console application loop. The class loads console storage state, reads terminal input, prints UI output, and also serves the JavaFX GUI.

That mix makes the class harder to read because console startup details sit beside GUI-facing response methods. The code quality guide recommends structuring code so each class has a clear purpose.

Let's move the console startup and input loop into BobbyConsole. Keep Bobby.main as a thin delegate so existing scripts that run bobby.Bobby continue to work.

This separates the front-end flow from the response engine without changing command behavior or introducing a larger application framework.

DateTimeParser uses null inside parseDateTime to mean that no supported date-time formatter matched the input.

That sentinel value makes the control flow less obvious because callers must know that null is a meaningful result rather than a missing object. The code quality guide recommends making code explicit and easy to read.

Let's return Optional from parseDateTime and use Optional.empty when no formatter matches. Add focused tests for supported formats, invalid input, and display formatting.

This keeps the public parse API unchanged because callers still receive a LocalDateTime or BobbyException. The Optional stays inside the parser where it documents the local fallback from date-time formats to date-only parsing.

TaskType defines the symbols used when tasks are displayed and saved. Storage repeats those same symbols when it reads tasks from the save file.

That duplication means a future change to a task type symbol must be made in more than one place. The code quality guide recommends avoiding duplicated logic and keeping related knowledge together.

Let's add symbol-to-type conversion to TaskType and let Storage use it when parsing saved task records. Keep Storage responsible for turning unknown symbols into the existing save-file error message.

This keeps the storage format unchanged while making TaskType the single source of truth for task type symbols.

commitResults.messageTitle: Use streams for task list transforms
commitResults.messageBody:
TaskList.find and Storage.saveTasks build new collections by manually iterating over the task list.

Those loops are simple collection transformations: one filters matching tasks, and the other maps tasks to their storage strings. Java streams express those transformations directly and keep the surrounding methods focused on their purpose.

Let's use streams for the matching-task filter and the storage-line mapping. Keep the return type of TaskList.find unchanged so existing callers continue to work.

This applies streams only where they improve readability. The parsing and command-handling code still uses ordinary control flow because those paths depend on validation and error handling.
